title: The ninth Guru's voice
hook: his hymns are short, calm and plain, about the passing world and the steady Name

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sangrand, and your line: every month is his. Did you call a hard day still His day? The Barah Maha is finished. Today a new block begins, and a new voice. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

Sikh tradition tells this story. In 1664 the boy Guru, Har Krishan, was dying in Delhi, and said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, a village in Punjab. Soon Bakala was full of men claiming to be Guru. Then a trader named Makhan Shah arrived. Caught in a storm at sea, he had vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru if his ship survived. It had. So he went from claimant to claimant, laying two coins before each. Each one took them, pleased. At last he found a quiet man who had made no claim at all. That man looked up and asked about the rest of the promise.
screen: `BAKALA, 1664: MANY CLAIMANTS.` → `MAKHAN SHAH'S VOW.` → `THE QUIET MAN WHO MADE NO CLAIM.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Makhan Shah ran up to the rooftop shouting that he had found the Guru. The quiet man was Tegh Bahadur, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, and he became the ninth Guru. He was born in 1621, and by then he had spent many years at Bakala in meditation. That stillness is all over his hymns. Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani was added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh. It's commonly counted as fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks, a short body of work next to Guru Arjan's. And it sounds different. The language leans toward Braj, the poetic speech of the region around Mathura, softer and more flowing than the Punjabi of the earlier Gurus. The hymns are short. They often begin by speaking straight to someone: saadho, holy ones, or man re, O mind. And they keep returning to two things. Everything we see is passing, like a dream or the shadow of a cloud. And the Name of the Lord is the one thing that stays. There's no anger in them. No fireworks. Just plain, calm sentences, the way an older friend talks to you when it matters. That calm wasn't a mood he had for poetry. Sikhs remember that in 1675 he gave his life in Delhi, refusing to bow under force, and his hymns are the voice of the man who walked toward that. For the next month, we'll listen to it: a voice that doesn't raise itself, and is very hard to forget.
screen: `THE QUIET MAN BECAME THE NINTH GURU.` · `FIFTY-NINE SHABADS, FIFTY-SEVEN SALOKS.` · `SAADHO, MAN RE: SPOKEN STRAIGHT.` · `PASSING WORLD, STEADY NAME.` · then, large: `CALM AND PLAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one of his shabads. If you can, find a recording of a shabad by Guru Tegh Bahadur, marked Mahalla nine, and play it now, eyes closed. Don't work at the meaning. Just listen to the pace of it, the plainness. If you can't play anything, sit quietly and imagine a voice that never hurries, saying something true. Notice what your own breath does when nothing is shouting at it. The bell holds the time.
The ninth Guru's voice. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are short, calm and plain: the passing world, and the steady Name.
Your line: calm and plain. Today, in one conversation that matters, try saying the true thing simply and slowly, without raising your voice to make it land. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 579 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GIVE UP PRIDE, HOLY ONES.`

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, marked Mahalla 9, are sung in kirtan across many ragas, and his saloks are read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're Makhan Shah. you vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru, and Bakala is full of claimants. what do you do?
options: give all five hundred to the first claimant you meet.
lay two coins before each and wait.
go home and keep the gold.
fork.reveal: tradition says he laid two coins before each. only the quiet man who made no claim asked about the rest of the vow, and Makhan Shah shouted from the rooftop that he had found the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: shabad, a hymn, the Guru's word. Guru Tegh Bahadur's are marked Mahalla 9.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ninth Guru is mainly known for how he died.
what it means: his short, calm hymns about the passing world and the steady Name are part of every Sikh's scripture.
what a scholar hears: his bani was not in Guru Arjan's 1604 Adi Granth; Sikh tradition holds that Guru Gobind Singh added it in the Damdama recension, about thirty years after his death.

sources.ref: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani, Mahalla 9 (Guru Granth Sahib, across fifteen ragas; Salok Mahalla 9, Ang 1426–1429)

notes: Counts of fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks are the common count; please confirm.
Bakala story told as tradition (claimants, two coins each, rooftop shout 'guru ladho re'); the number of claimants (often given as twenty-two) is left out deliberately.
Birth 1621, guruship 1664, death in Delhi 1675; the Damdama recension around 1705–06 is traditional: please check.
The description of his language as leaning toward Braj should be confirmed by a scholar.
